div.p: HE. HENRY GEORGE AND LAND NATIONALISATION. BY ECONOMIST."

A op will effort is bin 4 made jest now to spread the doctrine of Land Nationalisation in England. Mr. Henry George, who, though by no means the first to propose or to advocate the National owner- ship of land, may yet be regarded as the great apostle of that scheme of laud reformit: at present in , tins country, awl will we are told, during a stay of I three or four inonthi; carry on an active lecturing 1 propaganda. Already a successful start has TIMM made in the great metropolis, and backed up as Mr. George is by strong hotly a supporters, operations will soon be carried into the provinces. It is therefore not an inoppostune time to give a few details of the author of tt Progress and Poverty," and of the opinions as to to tke proper mode of dealing with the hind which he enunciates in his well-known book.

--Fi;;nt biographical scraps that have been made I, public from time to time I gather that Mr. George ' VlOl3 born in Chiladelphia in I0:19. Ile Man not Isoberest into the world with any of the advantages of wealthy parentage, and at the age of fourteen he I went into a counting house. After a short experi- ence of sea-faring life, we find him in California in I NM, and there lie worked as a compositor for the next seven or eight years. From the printer's care he gradually advanced himself to the editor's chair. and amongst other papers, he edited the S. Francisco- Times "and Fist." From 1576 to 1:479 he was the State Inspector of gas meters for Cali- fornia, and from 1079 to ISSO trustee of the San Francisco Free Public Library. In the latter year he removed to New York. where he has since resided. The present is not Mr. George's first visit to this country. Ile was here for a short period in 1001-2, and while paying a visit to Ireland. he was there arrested as a stuspoet," and was not released till he had given satisfactory proof of his identity, and of the innocence of his intentions. He was again in England in the latter part of 1003 and the beginning of ISM. and at that time he gave lectures in London and several of the most important pro- vincial towns, In his own country,and particularly in New York, Mr. George taken a prominent part in public life, and when about two years ago he was a candidate for the Mayoralty of the greatest city in the New World 110thillg aurprised his opponents to !much as the largeness of the number of votes that were polled in his favour.

If the importance of a hook m to be gauge I by its influence in moulding opinion on the sabjeot it deals with, there have been few more important honk than Mr. George's " Progress and Poverty " published in this century. In England its doctrines have permeated the public mind to a wondertul extent, and have, directly or indirectly, profoundly biased the discussion of land reform. There are !several members of Parliament who take more than no academic interest in land nationalisation, and , the recently-elected Council of London has within I the past week or two appointed a cothmit tee to ascertain the value of the land of the metropolis as distinct from the value of the houses and other buildings which are erected upon it—a distinctly Georgian project. It is said that in New Zealand Mr. Oeorge's teachings have already modified land legislation, and even in despotic RUNSIP Count , Tolstoi. the great writer, lion avowed himself a disciple of the American economist Like many another eventually successful book " Progress and Poverty' Was rejected of the publishers. It has teen stated that the book ma, composed whilst Mr. George was still a compositor, and that, not, being able to find a publisher who would undertake I its publication. be put it in type with his own hands. Not having the means to carry the work further it remainml in that condition for some years. and was not issued to the hook-reading world till 1g79. It is supposed that since then it has had a phenomen- ally large sale for a hook of its kind.
MR (MORON'S DOCTRINRS._

..... Of Malthus's " Essay an Pointlotion" it has been sairL—nne cannot help thinking in exaggerated language—that it " caused a cloud of pessimism to rest over the world." Referring to the sloctrine of Malthus, Macdonnel in his " Survey of Political Economy," says, "On those who have not familiarised themselves with the literature and controversy which Malthus originated it ie im- possible to impress any adequate sense of the ; fatalistic depression which this sMM rine, stkunder- I stood and misapplied, for a time produced—hove the depressing conclusion drawn from it unnerved the hands and damped the hearts of philanthropists." Malthus was a" clergyman, a Tory, and a friend of the government of the slay "and his object was to refute the arguments advanced by Godwin in his 0 Enquiry concerning Political Judice." Godwin argued that poverty an I misery wets caused by the imperfections and injusticea of human laws and institutions. Amend these, he said, nnd poverty and the vice, and misery which spring from poverty will ; disappear. Malt hue, on the other Irand, contended that poverty was not attributable to catr.es coer which governments and legislatures have any control. but to the tendeney in human beings to mffitiply their kind beyond the means of subsistence. ; If, he mist, you divide the whole of the annually ; produced wealth of a country in equal parts amongst its inhabitants there would no doubt for a . time he a general plenty. hut the ultimate result wnuld he that popolation would increase so much more rapidly than the means of subsistence that there would soon he an in,ufficiency of the necessaries of life. According to this view then the only effective way to better the condition of the people was, not to nisslslle with the laws and institutions of a country, but to restrain. ; by one Mettile or another, the growth of I population. It is hardly necessary to any that in this respect Mr. Henry Gwrge is a follower 1 of Godwin and not of Malthus. The terrible poverty, which, notwithstanding all the material I progress that has been and is being made, oppresses I modern nations like a nightmare is, he affirms, due not to excessive increase of population bid to al single human institistion —and that institution is . private ownership of land. div.p: we take the kernel. It is not necessary to confiscate land; it is only necessary to oonfiscate rent." In order to confiscate rent for the use of the State he ' proposes that all taxes should be almlished save one arm land values. This !logic land tax is to be kept so • high that it will sweep into the coffers of the State' to be used for the general good, nearly the whole of the annual value of the land of the country,leaving to ; the nominal owners only sufficient to induce them to retain possession and to undertake the trouble and responsibility of collection. Such, in brief, are some of the ideas which Mr. George will labour I during the next two or three months to popularise in England. To some the single /and tax may seem , , one of the most original proposals in Mr. George's j programme. Yet even here we have an exeellent ; illustration of the truth of the adage that there in nothing new under the sun. So far back as 1734, Jacob Tanderlint, a writer on economics, ins tract entitled," Money answers all things," advocated the single land tax m substitution of every other, and ! even then the suggestion was based upon bleu. Ithrown out many years before by the great Willow,- plies, Locke. About thirty years later than I Vanderlinis tract, Quesnay, an eminent Freneh man who is often spoken of as the real founder of Ihe science of political economy, promulgated what Adam Smith has designated his " liberal and generous system," a cardinal feature of which was a single Intel tax—an impot univto. Quesnay's prin- . ciples were received with enthusiasm by Turgot, the elder Mirabeau, and many other enlightened Frenchmen who were striving to alleviate the misery !of their countrymen—a misery which soon after culminated in the great Revolution. But the single- tax scheme made little progress at that time. The pre-Revolution nobility of France would NMI nothing to do with .* liberal and generous systems" which meant the taking of Rome of the accumulated !I bunkum from the backs of the poor and placing ! them on their own. The single tax proposal has already at the end of the nineteenth century I obtained a far wider acceptance than it over did ! towards the end of the eighteenth century. Its advocates now address themselves not to a narrow !, and selfish aristocracy but to a wide and all-power_ . flit democracy —to the landless and not to the . landed class.

LORD SALISBURY BpOEO St Watford, OR Tuesday, at an unhappy time for the Tory party, and he made an unhappy apecart. It was in the worst style of the toaster of flouts and gibes and jeers. It is scarcely oinceivable that a Prime Minister should be at re,kiess, resentful, and mendacious ; but it would seem that his lordship is losing his head through being too coma:ions of a lost cause. Be dislikes having to speak of Ireland, and yet his speech is full of Ireland. Ile flutters round the subject as the moth flutters round the candle, and hew likely to have the fate of the moth. Referring to the qacstion of the forged letters, Lord Sams- num- nays —"The fact that a man has forged your signature is no proof that you are possessed j of every statesmanlike quality and every ! moral virtue." Just an, but did anybody ever say it wadi' It is at least proof, in this particular case, that Mr. PARNELL is IVA guilty of inciting to end condoning assassination ; and one would think that the head of a party winch boasts of its" gentlemen' would at least express satisfac- ti.m that a foul charge had fallen baseless to the i ground. Wit the Prime Minister floes nothing of the kind ; he is like too many of his party—the MASS of his diaaatisfaction is that the elnrge has I net proved true. Indeed, with an audacity which is equalled only by its meanness, he procveds to treat the forged letters as if their forgery were still , an open question, for he says :—" Whatever may be the truth as to these documents, and it is very myaterions,whatever may be the truth with respect to them, whether they were forged or not, this alone is quite certain, that they were never pro- : duced by the Tory party." "The truth" indeed ! Is it not °neigh that Proorr confessed to their forgery when he found that forgery was being, p,. e/ ; and that ho ran away and committed I entente rather than face another day'a crow- examination h. Lord SALISBURY may protean, if he , likes, to ignore the exposure of the most gigantic freed of this generation; but it won't do. The conspiracy has been found out; the part the Govorneient have played in it is being found out; and they are sintering as a consequence the execration of mankind. Nor is it forgotten that for a long time the Tories iirlipantly made protest against the suggestion that any member of the Tory Cabinet had been closeted with Mr. PARNELL ;or that it NM 110 L Ilia Mr. GLABITONII had re- pettedly and plintelly rgerrefl to the subject, tint L ad SALISBURY confessed that Ire himself was privy to the negotiations which his Lmd-Lietitenant had with the leader of the Irish party. Now, Dr. liana is a setTant of the ,I State he has broken one of the rides of the !service in writing sech a letter; indeed be has • been reproved by the 110 MR SECRETARY for his I breach of discipline; and yet we have the fact !exposed that the Wan SECRETARY has been ii !party to this broach of discipline. In other words they wore set to work by the Government to help bigot up the case for the "Times," for Mr. BALFOUR admitted, with an air ,of injured innocence, that he supposed the idols. motion won supplied to the " Times." But the most damaging point was made by Mr. Hasty who naked whether Mr. HORNE had not been pro- Hnoted in consequence of the assistance he had rendered to the "Times." The IRISH SECRETARY mild not deny this promotion, or that it had I taken place since thin special work; all he could any was that the promotion,wss not inconsequence of the assistante he had rendered. " Braes Mr. !" How he shrunk within himself on Monday evening! hut the whirligig of time has only begun to bring in its revmiges. Thin Govern- ment, with their Intim SECRETARY, have sown the wind, and they have yet to reap the whirlwind.

The twelfth animal report of the Female Strangers' Lodging House situate at nlO5, Picea- dilly, Manchester, has just lieen issued, and it is obvious that good work is being done. The total on the register for last year was 1,074, and as many an .524 strangers stayed for one night only. An institution such as this is invaluable in a large town. It was established by Dr. Fraser, the Into 'Bishop of Manchester.

A journeyman printer named Wheadon,on being sued in London, the other day, plesded that h., courtmhip had been of " the rambling kind," by which, he said, he meant walking oat together to . see d anything would come of it. Unfortnnately, ,1 he had madded, too, in the matter of correspond- ! once, mid had " filled nut a line" with crosses, which were taken to mean kisses. His rambling went too for, and something did come of it—an order to pay 4:20 by way of compensation.

The Rev. T. W. Twainley, formerly a curate at Dewsbury and Wakefield, has been sent to gaol for six months for presenting a forged cheque. His conneel, at Leeds Assizes, on Monday, pleaded in his behalf that he had " got mixed up with polities," and polities are, to be sure, sometimes , very demoralizing. I;nt it was more to the point that it was also admitted that he got mixed up with whisky. He had hail seventeen glasses on , the day of the fraud, and seventeen glasses are surely sufficient to demoralize a curate —apart : fronts being " mixed up with polities."

THE RAILWAY COMPANIES have got the start in the matter of high charges for the carriage of goods, and they will keep it if great pressure in not brought to bear 1111011 Parliament. In view of the possible restrictions of the Railway and , Canal Traflie Act, it would seem that, prior to the beginning of this year, the Railway Companies made alterations, or, to be more specific, raised their charges in certain cases. Their explanation is that the charges were revised to get rid of undue preference, and to cancel obsolete through rates, lint the through rates could scarcely have boon olsolete, or we should not so EOM have had complaints an to increased charges. In addition, notices have been given of increases of tariff ender the Act, amounting in some cases to from 40 to 100 per cent. Naturally traders, manufacturer., and agriculturists are up in arms against what seems like a determined assault lipon their interests. The Warrington Chamber of Coma/twee are formulating their objections; yesterday the matter was before the Widnes Local heard: and on Monday next tho Newton Improvement Commissioners are to meet certain tradesmen of the district in order that joint action 11114 y Ile taken. On Tuesday, there wasa meet- ing in Manchester, of the Lancashire and Cheshire IConference on Railway Rates and Charges; and on the inotion of the Town Clerk of Blackburn it was resolved: —" That objections to the proposals of the railway companies be sent in, as required by the Act, to Om Board of Trade, together with copies, ES required, to the secretaries of the res- pective companies, within the limit of time fixed by the Board of Trade; and tliat menilwra of the Consultative Committee are hereby requested to at once tarnish the chairman of the confer- ence with particulars of any emelt objections." It will he seen that the tusale with the Railway Companies is likely to he a sharp, if not a long one The fact should not he lest flight of that the Com- panies are wealthy and well-organised, and that they know how to make their influence felt in, Parliament. It is a mathar of course to say that members of the House of Commons are as a rule holders of railway shares; but they will not stand idly by and pine injustice done if they aro made to feel that their constituents require them to look Ito the banned.. of the public rather than to their own. The issue ions important and far-reaching I, as to demand incessant vigilance, and prompt , action.

We are not only misgoverning Ireland but doing it at an absurd cost. It trampires from the Civil Service .timativt that the cost of the Irish constabulary is £1,419,371 ; the cost for England and Wales is £l,4iiçsis; that is to say, we are expending, roundly speaking, as much on the government of the five millions of people in Ire- land as upon the twenty-six millions in England and Wales. Add to the total for Ireland the amount spent, in addition, upon the soldiery, and it will be seen our financial folly borders on mad-1

The Liberal Unionist M.P.'s are in the Govern- meet boat ; they sink or swim together. Bet storms sometimes unexpectedly arise, and they may sink before 1893.

EMBEZZLEMENT AT WARRINGTON.
WESLEYAN QUARTERLY 3IEETING.

The March quarterly 'netting of the Warrington Wesleyan Circuit was held on Monday evening, in the Bold-at. Nest ry, there being a very large Eaten- dance of stewards and other officers. Am fngst those present were Sle,srs. Si!cock and Ilenshall, ! circuit stewards; Dr. Boman. Councillor J. Shaw- I , Breen, Messrs. E. Richardson, J. Bennett, R. Cook.; and D. lianiett. The financial statement was read ; by the circuit stewards and showed that, after pay- ing all charges against the circuit, there was a balance againg, the stewards of a little over £2. This I ; statement was considered to be eminently. satisfactory, I ' as some extraordinary expenditure had lawn thrown on the On uit (hiring the quarter. Tile statement of Illetn- bership, which was n-ad by the superintendent minister I [ (the Rev. G. E. Cook, J. tillaw-lirecti, S. tteoaett,arst he” ot, Mr. B i Brooks was nvited to remain a third year. This invitation was acknowledged and acceded to by Mr. Brooks in feeling terms. A similar vote of thanks and invitation, together with a special vote of condolence on the Ita): it his wife, wore roared to the Rev. E. Jackwm who, after thanking the meeting for their kindness to him, consented to remain a third year. GORTON ELECTION.

At (melon, on Tuesday morning, Mr. Ernest Hatch (Conservative, and Mr. William Mather Hiladitonian Liberal) were nominated is candidatea for the vacancy in the Parliamentary representation of the Gorton Divo sion of South-East Lancashire, ontsol by the death of Mr. Richard Peacock (Gladstonian Liberal). Mr. Gladstone has written a letter con:mantling the candidature of Mr. Mather, and anticipating that the I constituency will show that it is in sympathy with the movement of opposition which nosy prevails in the I country and which promises to bring the Irish ondros I versy to a close. M. Mather, the Liberal candidata for the representa- tion of Gorton, add:vs:mai:l crowded meeting on Wednes- ! day evening_ in the People's Hall, Denton. He svas accompanied be Sir Wilfrid Lawson. who urged Liberals to spare no eflirt to sector a substantial ma;ority en the I polling day. Mr. Penwick. M.P., and other gentlemen al. spoke. A meeting M Gorton was addreseed by Mr. Pierre Mabony, M.P., Mr. F. S. Stevenson, M.P., and: other mmtlemen. The nommen,. of Local Opti.b in the I , division heldn largo meeting in the Crossley Hall, at I Opensbaw. and passed a resolution in support of Mr.i hlather's candidature. Meetings were also held in the ! interest of the Conservative candidate. I Polling ,kontnenerd yesterday morning in the Gorton I Division. The votes will to, counted this (Saturday) . I morning, and the resnit ii espected lo Ire declared about noon. Carriages of every kind were plentiful, and the election proceedill briskly, though perfect order 'me- i coiled. MUNICIPAL DEPUTATIONS. Sir,— nem* allow me to waif. 1 have to-day incidentally heard it remarlud that the Mayor, Town Clerk, and Bornugh Treasnrer ,ff Warrington ore up in London, or down in London, just as you preter to have it, at present, in connection suit, seme meetings of municipal corporations that are being held in the big city. I hove no objection to make , to this nor to the fact that there have been sundry l deputations at various times undortaking journeys in connection with the sanitary department, for presumably the ratepayers get value for such visits. I think, how- I ever, that as the nubilo pay the piper, they should be I let "into the know" a little bit more, and I would most I respectfully suggest that there would be no harm , done license enterprising member of the Corporation were to put specific inquiries as to the accounts thus incurred when they come forward, so that the public may be satisfied that these " offs' ore something better than little picnics planned in the interests of those who take part in them.—Yours, &c., WANT TO KNOW. THE LINCOLN CASE. Sir,—We think there must be a very large number of Churchmen throughout the country who would be glad of an r pporlunity for showing some practical sympathy with the promoters in the Lincoln Carie, who hove taken each a bold stand in defence of the Protestant character of our National Church. Their action will distinctly clerk, the law as to the power of a bishop to introduce (for the first time since the Reformation) ceremonies alreedy ascertsinwl to he unlawful in the Me of an inferb r clergyman. The institution of these proceedings insoles, a very heavy pecuniary responsibility, which cc ff., I sure loyal members of th, Church of England will he pleased to share, and for this purpose we offer to west, the help of those who sympathize with them. ! Sidweriptions, whether large or small, may be for- warded to either of us, or paid to our account at the Barclay, Bevan lc Co., 54, Lemhard- f• Tour obedient Servants, BLACKWOOD, Shortlands House, Sl.rtlands, Kent.
